statement: Let \(ABCD\) be a quadrilateral with \(\angle DAB = 60^\circ\), \(\angle ABC = 90^\circ\), and \(\angle BCD = 120^\circ\). The diagonals \(AC\) and \(BD\) intersect at point \(M\). Given that \(BM = 15\) and \(MD = 30\), determine the area of quadrilateral \(ABCD\).

Determine all positive integers \(n\) for which
\[n - \lfloor n\{\sqrt{n}\} \rfloor = 2,\]
where \(\lfloor x \rfloor\) and \(\{x\}\) denote, respectively, the integer part and the fractional part of the real number \(x\) they enclose.

Note: For example, \(\lfloor 5.7 \rfloor = 5\) and \(\{5.7\} = 0.7\).

Let \(k\) be an odd integer greater than 1. On a table there are \(k\) piles of stones: the first has 1 stone, the next has 2 stones, the next has 3 stones, and so on until the last, which has \(k\) stones. In the first step, 3 piles are chosen and all their stones are combined into a new pile, from which 1 stone is removed. In the second step, 3 piles are chosen and all their stones are combined into a new pile, from which 2 stones are removed. In general, in step \(n\), 3 piles are chosen and all their stones are combined into a new pile, from which \(n\) stones are removed. After several steps, only a single pile remains on the table, containing \(p\) stones.

a. Prove that \(p\) is a perfect square if and only if the numbers \(2k+2\) and \(3k+1\) are perfect squares.

b. Find the minimum value of \(k\) for which \(p\) is a perfect square.

Note: In each step, the stones that are removed are discarded permanently.

Let \(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{100}\) and \(b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_{100}\) be 200 distinct real numbers. On a \(100 \times 100\) board, the number \(a_i + b_j\) is written in the cell of row \(i\) and column \(j\). It turns out that in each column, the product of the 100 numbers is equal to 1. Prove that in each row, the product of the 100 numbers is equal to \(-1\).

On the real line, 22 points are marked:
\[0 \leq a_1 < a_2 < a_3 < \cdots < a_{21} < a_{22} \leq 1.\]
The allowed operation is to choose any two marked points \(A\) and \(B\), erase them, and mark their midpoint. Prove that, regardless of the initial configuration of the 22 points, it is possible to perform 20 allowed operations so that the distance between the only two remaining points is at most \(0.001\).

Note: Assume that in each operation, the midpoint of \(AB\) does not coincide with any already marked point.
